scenario: A central-government policy fellowship shortlists applicants if they have either exceptional data-analysis skill or exceptional Hindi-policy-writing skill. Additionally, 5% of applicants with neither trait are admitted through a regional-diversity wildcard. Observers notice that shortlisted candidates strong in data analysis seem weak in Hindi writing.

data.description: The shortlist is selected on either of two strengths plus a small wildcard from the neither group.

question: Among shortlisted applicants, compute (a) P(data-analysis | Hindi-writing, shortlisted), and (b) P(data-analysis | not Hindi-writing, shortlisted). Compare the shortlist association with the population relationship and identify the mechanism.

ground_truth.explanation: The two skills are independent in the population, but shortlisting on either skill induces a spurious negative association in the shortlisted set.

naive_answer: Shortlisted candidates who are strong in Hindi writing seem less likely to be strong in data analysis, so the two skills must conflict.
naive_trap: This is collider bias from selection on either skill. Among shortlisted applicants lacking Hindi-writing skill, most were selected because they had strong data-analysis skill.
reasoning_trace: Step 1: P(data | Hindi, shortlisted) = 2160/18000 = 0.12. Step 2: Among not-Hindi shortlisted applicants, data-only = 9840 and wildcard neither = 3608, so P(data | not Hindi, shortlisted) = 9840/(9840+3608) = 0.7317. Step 3: The negative association is induced by the shortlist rule, not by the population.
